message.content: {"skills": [{"category": "characterization", "trigger": "When evaluating chest radiographs with peripheral lung opacities to distinguish chronic eosinophilic pneumonia from other interstitial or inflammatory lung diseases.", "steps": ["Inspect the distribution of opacities on PA and lateral views, specifically checking for involvement of the outer third of the lung fields (subpleural/peripheral zone).", "Assess the vertical distribution to determine if there is a predilection for the upper lobes or apices.", "Evaluate the density and margins; look for non-segmental, fluffy, or consolidation-like opacities that spare the central perihilar regions.", "Distinguish from pulmonary edema by confirming the pattern is the 'photographic negative' (peripheral/apical) rather than the classic central/bat-wing distribution.", "Differentiate from organizing pneumonia (which is often patchy, migratory, and less strictly peripheral/apical) and sarcoidosis (which typically presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules rather than peripheral consolidation)."]}]}
